findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks binary/source compatibility for existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public SPI interface. Adding `int order();` as a plain abstract method (no default implementation) means any third-party or external implementation of CryptoProvider that does not implement order() will fail to compile/load (AbstractMethodError at runtime for compiled classes). Since CryptoProvider is loaded via ServiceLoader and is explicitly designed to allow multiple implementations on the classpath (per this PR's own rationale), existing external providers will break. A default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would preserve backward compatibility while still allowing the new ordering feature.

findings.title: Multiple-provider conflict is now silently resolved instead of failing fast
findings.body: Previously, detecting more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath threw an IllegalStateException, forcing the user to fix a misconfigured/ambiguous classpath. Now the code silently picks the provider with the highest order() value and only logs the ignored ones at debug level (which is often disabled in production). If two providers happen to have the same order() value (e.g. DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider both return 200), the selection becomes non-deterministic (dependent on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order), which can silently select the wrong crypto backend (e.g., non-FIPS instead of FIPS) without any error, which is a serious regression for environments that require strict crypto provider guarantees.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() does not actually return a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: The implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. whatever JCA provider backs the JVM's default keystore type (typically the JDK's built-in provider, not BouncyCastle). This contradicts the documented contract of the method ("BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider") and is misleading for any caller (e.g. via BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER in the common module) that assumes the returned provider name/behavior matches a BC-compatible provider. This could cause obscure NoSuchProviderException or incorrect algorithm resolution wherever generic code paths (not overridden with UnsupportedOperationException in this class) rely on this provider.

findings.title: Dead/leftover code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) whose results are discarded and have no effect on the method's output - the actual DER sequence is built again right afterwards on lines 117-121. This is clearly leftover debugging/refactoring code that should be removed; it wastes allocations and makes the method harder to review/maintain.

findings.title: Inconsistent use of format.name() instead of format.toString() for KeyStore lookup
findings.body: getKeyStore() calls `KeyStore.getInstance(format.name())`, whereas every other CryptoProvider implementation in this PR (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) consistently uses `format.toString()`. If KeystoreUtil.KeystoreFormat overrides toString() to return a value different from the enum constant name() (which is a common pattern for such enums, e.g. to map to the exact JCA keystore type string), this implementation will request a different/incorrect keystore type than intended, potentially throwing KeyStoreException at runtime for formats where name() and toString() diverge.

findings.title: No test coverage for the new provider-ordering/selection logic
findings.body: The detectProvider() method's behavior changed significantly: it now sorts providers by order() and silently picks the highest, logging the rest. There is no unit test added in this PR verifying that, given multiple CryptoProvider implementations with different order() values on the classpath, the correct (highest-order) one is selected, nor a test for the tie-break behavior when two providers share the same order(). This is core logic for the stated goal of the PR (allowing multiple CryptoProvider instances) and should be covered by a dedicated test.
